item.title: MAGA is having a normal one
item.description: Also: The online stans-turned-political-prisoners and ...is Threads back?
item.content:encoded:
By Jeremiah Johnson

Welcome to The Weekly Scroll!

The Weekly Scroll is a once-a-week roundup of the most interesting, strangest, and funniest stories from around the social internet.

This week, we’re talking about the online Right’s collective freakout, how Threads still hasn’t become a thing, and why stan accounts keep ending up as political prisoners.

The Right’s no-good, very bad week

It’s not the best time to be a MAGA soldier online. Poll after poll shows that Democrats are massive favorites to take back a majority in the House of Representatives next month, and they’re increasingly viewed as favorites to take back the Senate as well. The Argument/Split Ticket model currently gives Democrats an 89% chance of winning the House, and a 61% chance of taking the Senate. Trump’s approval is now at -26 with likely voters. It’s hard out there!

Surely the online Right has cooked up some fantastic responses, right? What have the loyal patriots of the MAGA machine been doing as the electorate turns on them?

Well, Chris Rufo — the Manhattan Institute fellow famous for kicking off the right’s war on critical race theory — decided to devote a full episode of his podcast to “The Indian Question.” The “question” at hand is literally just the existence of Indian Americans and whether or not white people should feel disgusted by them. I watched the entire 72-minute podcast so you don’t have to (and you gremlins better subscribe to The Argument because god knows I’m not doing that for free), and it’s as bad as you’d suspect something echoing the Jewish Question would be.

Rufo, along with his co-host Jonathan Keeperman — better known as @L0m3z on Twitter, where he’s argued that best response to the left is “shut up fag“ — argued at various points that Indians can never assimilate as long as anyone can notice that they’re different, that racism against non-white Americans is actually good because it’s a form of “hazing,” and that meritocracy is probably a flawed idea because Indians keep winning the spelling bee.

Subscribe now

The typical exchange is Rufo trying to launder white nationalist talking points with some more reasonable-sounding justification, followed by an objection from Keeperman that no, let’s be very clear, we just think the Indians are gross and don’t need to have a reason why. Rufo then typically gives a little “this crazy guy!” grin, concedes the point and moves on. I wish I was making any of this up.

Keeperman: There are a lot of people for whom… the preference to live in a homogeneous society… there’s not like some rational reason necessarily for it. They just like it better in the way that certain people like certain kinds of foods better. They don’t owe a kind of reasoned explanation for why they prefer a slice of pizza to a burrito or something.

Which makes sense, because being disgusted by another race of person is exactly like preferring pizza to burritos.

The episode drew significant pushback in conservative circles, probably because it was 25% too open about the kind of white nationalism that lurks under the surface of so much modern right-wing politics. But Rufo’s podcast wasn’t the only racial controversy this week — the right also had a miniature war over whether or not it was anti-white racism for Sarah Huckabee Sanders to air an ad depicting a white man on welfare.

And far-right Twitter personality @Howlingmutant0 — best known for racist, misogynistic, and antisemitic jokes that have attracted the attention of followers like Vice President JD Vance — was stunned that after years of cultivating a fanbase of white nationalists, he faced a revolt from that fanbase after it was revealed he has a mixed-race child.

But hey! This is all just internet stuff, podcasts and influencers. Maybe right-wingers in office are doing better.

Jack Smith, the former special counsel in charge of investigating Donald Trump, was on the Hill this week to defend his scrutiny of the president before Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee. The title of the hearing was “Oversight of Jack Smith’s Abuse of Authority and the Targeting of Republicans and Related Matters.”

It all went south for Republicans during questioning by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., whose inquiries about whether Smith attended an Atlanta Hawks basketball game completely fell apart.

The questioning was meant to somehow establish that Smith had improper ties to Georgia prosecutor Fani Willis, who indicted Trump in a separate state case over alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election. Schmitt is visibly grinning to himself during the exchange, revealing texts Smith’s staff sent about attending a basketball game.“I don’t think you know that we have this stuff,” Schmitt says smugly before accusing Smith of perjury.

What a bombshell!1 But wait! It turns out that some poor staffer made a mistake. They either forgot that women’s basketball exists, or confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes, as Smith confirmed that he was actually at a women’s college basketball game between Maryland and Iowa, and nowhere near Atlanta.

The moment was so humiliating it spawned the first ever Congressional Surrender Cobra.2

What makes the entire thing so funny is how utterly confident Schmitt was that he had a major, blockbuster scandal to reveal. It’s common to build a press strategy to try and amplify big moments in Congress. Right as Schmitt’s line of questioning was falling apart, conservative influencers were tweeting seemingly pre-prepared talking points. After the hearing, Schmitt had a recording of the Charlie Kirk Podcast lined up to celebrate his big win, and bumbled his way through it without ever acknowledging he got the only fact that mattered completely wrong. And Schmitt had, just that morning, been pumped up by Axios as a potential VP candidate for 2028. RIP to Schmitt’s VP chances (Born Sept 29th, died Sept 29th).

Things went no better on Pennsylvania Avenue: The White House deputy chief of staff posted a six-second clip that may have been thinly veiled QAnon signalling while the president tried to rebrand AI as SI (superintelligence).3

But this is all dude stuff — I bet at least the right’s women are being normal! Haha, no, the big women’s stories out of MAGA this week are a conspiracy that Candace Owens is a secret lesbian and an article about an anti-feminist “groypette” who was shocked, shocked when her groypers turned on her.

Why is MAGA being overrun by scandals, insane nonsense, and infighting? This is what happens when a party is facing electoral disaster and knows it. The political media is having a field day writing article after article about Republican midterm panic. The war with Iran remains toxically unpopular, the price of gas is still high, and there’s little good news to focus on. Small wonder that the online right is collapsing into failed conspiracy theories, racist nonsense, and back-stabbing.

Gaga Daily was in jail

The X account @GaGaDaily was like any other popular stan account: posting videos, memes, and more about Lady Gaga to an audience of almost half a million followers. But in February of 2024, the account suddenly went silent for more than a year. Now, we finally know what happened:

The New York Times has more detail — the account belongs to a Belarussian man named Kirill, who was arrested in February 2024 for participating in 2020 anti-government protests. He spent two years in a Belarussian prison before being released, and he now lives abroad. Lady Gaga, disappointingly, has not commented.

Oddly, this isn’t the first time a stan account creator has found themselves jailed for geopolitical stances. In 2019, a Taylor Swift fan account announced they’d been inactive for about two months because they were jailed for refusing to join the Israeli Defense Forces.

Subscribe now

Stop trying to make Threads happen

These days, there’s a specific type of story that gets written a couple of times per year. I don’t know if there’s a Central Bureau of Promoting Threads or if it’s just irresistible, but every so often, we get the “guys, Threads is really happening this time!” article. This week, it’s from Wired, who declares that Black Twitter is thriving on Threads.

For some reason, journalists keep trying to make this particular brand of fetch happen. They point out that Threads hit 500 million monthly active users this summer. They compare it to Reddit. They seem very eager for Threads to break out.

Yes, Threads has a lot of “users.” But while that metric is kind of real, it’s also kind of fake. Threads is heavily integrated with Instagram and Facebook, and many of its “active users” are people who accidentally click through to Threads content while on those other apps. The hottest meme on Threads this summer was “Richard has passed,” which is a joke about how lots of Facebook users are posting on Threads without even realizing they’re doing it.

So while Threads technically has users, it seems to be a fully vaporware userbase. They don’t spend any time there. Check out this graph of average daily time spent by active Android-app users by social network:

Threads is losing to Pinterest and LinkedIn!

More than just not being an app where people spend any real amount of time, Threads also doesn’t generate culture. Love it or hate it, Twitter is still essential for understanding online culture and politics, and it still has a remarkable density of people whose posts go on to become major news cycles or generate cultural discourse. Threads has none of that. The quality of content there is so bad that the tech writer Max Read dubbed it the “gas-leak social network.”

That’s probably why only 3% of Americans say they get news from Threads, a number so low that it runs into the Lizardman’s Constant. When was the last time someone showed you an awesome Threads meme? When was the last time an important cultural moment happened on Threads? Has it ever? I’m begging you all, stop. Stop trying to make Threads happen. It’s not going to happen.

Links

  • TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama $100 million in another instance of a social media company settling with a state government over claims of social media harms to children. As part of the settlement, TikTok also agreed to a number of product changes like time limits for teens, nighttime usage restrictions, a default non-personalized feed, and a ban on cosmetic filters for teens.

  • Pop singer Sia has sold a 50% stake in her musical catalog for $180 million. These deals are becoming more and more popular, and are part of a phenomenon I’ve written about before: Older, previously released art is smothering new art.

  • The Hollywood Reporter, in addition to tracking broadcast TV, streaming hits, and box office grosses, is now tracking the internet’s most popular microdramas.

  • I have been having an unreasonable amount of fun playing “Unusual Suspects”, a game where you do police sketches of various fictional characters.

  • Mattel released a “Hanukkah Barbie,” and it went poorly.

  • Caleb Hammer’s humiliation economy

Posts

  • A very good cat costume

  • Historical reenactment

  • Woke university

  • Who cares about existential risk anyway?

  • Are you wearing…

Subscribe now

1

Sidenote: It’s not even clear what this ‘bombshell’ would have proven. That Smith and Fani Willis were … in the same city on the same day? Okay?

2

I also strongly recommend this incredible view of Alabama Senator Katie Britt, who looks like she’s having ‘Nam flashbacks as she realizes what’s happening.

3

It’s also been alleged that insiders may have scooped up prominent .si domain names ahead of the announcement.

item.title: Americans want Congress to stop the imperial presidency
item.content:encoded:
By Kobe Yank-Jacobs

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

According to both President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, what the U.S. military is doing in Iran is not a war. That said, as of Friday, the U.S. is moving an additional 10,000 troops and a third aircraft carrier to the region, raising concerns that this suspiciously warlike “conflict” could escalate.

By all accounts, Americans are sick of the conflict, which was started unilaterally by the president. According to new data, they are also ready for Congress to rein it in.

Sixty-six percent of registered voters in The Argument’s latest poll, fielded nationally between September 16th and 22nd, believe that the president should be required to get Congressional approval before sending armed forces into action — and only 21% oppose. Almost a majority would go even further: 50% of voters believe that Congress should defund a military action when the president moves ahead without Congressional approval. (Only 26% of respondents oppose this.) Historically, the main enabler of unilateral presidential warmaking has been legislators’ skittishness about reigning in conflicts after they’ve started, but our survey suggests that this is a step that voters feel they are entitled to take.

Subscribe now

Now, it would be great if this result was motivated by high-minded respect for the Constitution, which is very clear that Congress is the branch with the power “to declare war,”1 but a closer look at the results suggests the results are heavily influenced by current events. For one, the current war in Iran — initiated unilaterally by President Trump — is the most unpopular war since Vietnam, when compared to Afghanistan, Iraq, and World War II. More voters think that George W. Bush’s invasion of Iraq was justified than the current conflict.

There is also a strong partisan slant to our poll results: 94% of people who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 said they think that Congress should approve war, while only 40% of Trump voters said the same. That said, 44% of Trump voters ages 30 to 44 preferred requiring Congressional approval, suggesting younger generations may be closer to consensus on the need for Congressional approval.2

But even if our results reflect anxieties specific to this moment in time, the overwhelming support for Congressional signoff is still a rebuke of what’s become business-as-usual in Washington.

The United States has not actually declared war since World War II. Beginning with the Korean War in 1950, presidents have either ordered troops into combat unilaterally, secured a different form of wartime “authorization” (as George W. Bush did to invade Afghanistan), or plainly abused past authorizations to make war elsewhere. (The Afghanistan authorization was used to justify drone strikes in Yemen and Somalia.) The result is that presidents functionally make war wherever and whenever they want.

In 1991, when asked what he would do if Congress declined to authorize the Gulf War, President George H.W. Bush told a reporter, “I still feel that I have the constitutional authority” — a sentiment later echoed by presidents from Barack Obama to Donald Trump.3

Thankfully, we don’t necessarily need high-minded Constitutionalism to change how things are done. Some of the most substantial reforms to presidential authority have come in response to specific presidents violating a norm or law, including term limits (after FDR), anti-nepotism laws (after JFK), and restrictions on withholding congressionally appropriated funds (after Nixon).

Congressional capitulation

The fact that half of registered voters are open to Congress taking action even after a president moves ahead with a war unilaterally could be the key to reigning in the executive here.

Once presidents take the initiative to launch a combat operation, it’s hard for politicians in Congress to take a vote opposing or reversing it. There is a fundamental asymmetry between a single person with the ability to handle threats quickly and a large deliberative body, lumbering along in its approval, each politician fearful of being seen as unpatriotic. That’s how war powers got out of whack in the first place: The history of U.S. warmaking is the president using dramatic incidents — real or provoked or lied about — to cow Congress into going along.

As early as 1846, James Polk ordered troops into disputed territory between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande to provoke the start of the Mexican-American War. To stir up support for the Spanish-American war in 1898, President William McKinley pointed to the explosion of a ship off the coast of Havana, despite inconclusive evidence about the cause of the explosion. (Later evidence has suggested it may have been an internal issue, not an attack).

In the summer of 1964, the Johnson administration claimed that its ships were innocently patrolling international waters when struck by the North Vietnamese, but they were really 12 miles off the Vietnamese coast, likely trying to draw fire. (The second of the alleged strikes also never happened.)

The modern era has made this dynamic — presidents making war a fait accompli and daring Congress to pull them back — much worse. In 1973, in the waning days of the Vietnam War, Congress tried to restrain presidents by passing the War Powers Resolution. The law generally required presidents to get congressional approval within 60 days or end hostilities, with up to 30 additional days if necessary for a safe withdrawal. But presidents have used that deadline to justify acting unilaterally.

Unfortunately, the law has had the opposite of its intended effect. On paper, it cemented the requirement for Congressional signoff. In practice, it gave presidents the green light for monthslong deployments that sitting members of Congress would end up hesitant to rein in.

The real significance of The Argument’s finding, even if it was heavily motivated by the current war on Iran, may be that the public believes Congress can act forcefully after a president has initiated combat, which is where we most need Congress to be muscular. If the issue is that legislators find it politically untenable to go against a war once it’s started, we now know that, in the abstract at least, the public is on their side.

The founders understood that excessive warmaking would not be due to the flawed character of this or that president but endemic to the office. That’s why they gave the power to Congress. It just so happens that this separation of powers is especially important when a president with a flawed character does take the helm.

Subscribe now

Midterm update

Lakshya Jain, our director of political data, uses data from The Argument’s polling operation to inform the Split Ticket 2026 House and Senate models. Here’s his update on the state of play this week:

Democrats remain the firmest of favorites to win the House, thanks to an environment that is even more favorable than it was in 2018: Their win probability is 89%. In the Senate, Democrats have a slight edge, with a 60% chance of winning the chamber thanks to leads in Alaska, Texas, Ohio, and North Carolina. Maine and Iowa are both tossup races, but Democrats only need to flip four of these six to take the chamber. Right now, polling and fundamentals are both so good for them that they’ve got a better-than-even chance of doing exactly that.

These models update every day; bookmark this page to see the odds of each party taking the House and the Senate.

Top stories this week, by Milan Singh

Nikole Hannah-Jones nearly broke the internet with a viral New York Times essay about sending her daughter to one of New York City’s worst-performing schools. While many of her conclusions drew criticism from education experts, there is one point on which Kelsey Piper found herself in firm agreement: Schools around the country are making it more and more difficult for parents to actually evaluate their children’s academic performance — and it’s not only because of grade inflation.

The Argument also released its latest national survey, which focused on how American voters think about war. Lakshya Jain, our director of political data, introduced the findings by highlighting just how incredibly unpopular Trump’s Iran war is with our respondents. Our polling shows that it’s nearly as unpopular as the Vietnam War, which killed over 58,000 Americans. And it’s even less popular than George W. Bush’s invasion of Iraq.

As a liberal, it’s tempting to stay out of public debates about the ultimate ends of human life. Liberal societies need to be able to accommodate private religious and spiritual codes that promote competing visions on this front. But in evading these questions, do we end up ceding ground to those who would degrade not just the political processes we value, but also the moral systems we privately hold dear? In his column this week, Matt Yglesias argues that while liberalism should remain neutral, liberals themselves need to take a stand on bigger questions than they may be comfortable with.

🌟Abundance Wins of the Week🌟

  • Top Senate Democrats and Republicans released the long-awaited text of a massive reform to the federal permitting regime: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAJAA). If passed, the package would make it much easier to build energy projects of all types — but likely with particularly pronounced benefits for clean energy — plus the long-distance transmission needed to efficiently move energy across the country.

  • In other good climate news, the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) issued a construction permit for the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) to build America’s first commercial small modular nuclear reactor. It’s the NRC’s second approval of construction for a new reactor this year, and both reviews were completed months ahead of schedule. Small modular reactors promise much simpler and faster paths to carbon-free nuclear energy than traditional reactors. (TVA will still need a separate operating license before it can run the reactor.)

  • New York City just unveiled 12 “Fast Track Districts” where it will streamline the review process for qualifying affordable housing projects. The districts — which include Manhattan’s Upper East and Upper West Sides, as well as large swaths of South Brooklyn, Staten Island, and Queens — were selected because they have produced the smallest share of the city’s affordable housing over the past five years: just 1% combined. The fast track process, which was approved by the city’s voters last year, is projected to reduce review times from seven months to three.

    Subscribe now

Worth watching…

There is a spectre haunting Europe: The far-right is on the rise. The AfD just placed first in the Saxony-Anhalt state elections in Germany. Reform UK is projected to come second in the next British general election. France will elect a new president next year, and the polling suggests that Marine Le Pen (or her acolyte Jordan Bardella) is the favorite to win.

Why is this happening? Is it the refusal of the center-left to make compromises on immigration? Or is it the refusal of the left to let people have air conditioning? Matt and Jerusalem discuss all this and more in the latest episode of The Argument podcast.

The only independent in the House of Representatives is waging a lonely fight against the gerrymandering arms race, which both political parties have escalated this cycle. Rep. Kevin Kiley, a former Republican who recently left the party after his district was redrawn, spoke with Lakshya Jain, The Argument’s director of political data, and Zachary Donnini about his decision and the polarization that gerrymandering encourages. “If you fight fire with fire, then the whole world burns,” he said. “There’s absolutely no reason that you should deprive your own citizens of fair representation based upon what some other state is doing.”

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Milan Singh

It’s officially October, and I’m ready for it: no more humidity, layering of outfits, assorted pumpkin spice foods and beverages. What can I say? I’m a bit basic.

To celebrate the arrival of autumn, I asked my esteemed colleagues for their fall-themed recommendations.

“I have no justification for how this is fall themed, but a friend found me in a Little Free Library The Floating Admiral, a detective novel collaboratively written by Agatha Christie, GK Chesterton, and twenty of their Golden Age detective novelist friends,” said staff writer Kelsey Piper. “It was great fun, and now I’m suffering immensely from the fact no one else I know has read it so that I can complain about it with them, so if you have read it, hit me up!”

Kelsey also read John LeCarre’s The Constant Gardener, but “while I love John LeCarre for being the most cynical everything-is-bad-because-of-human-nature-and-always-will-be spy novelist of them all, it hits differently when he’s being cynical about post-colonial Kenya instead of declining imperial Britain, so it was mostly just kind of depressing.”

Gender and culture fellow Maibritt Henkel recommended Julia Jacklin’s new album The Gem, which she said was “perfect for October — think Australian Phoebe Bridgers.” Operations manager Angela Tracy overcame some initial difficulty in narrowing the recommendations down (because “fall is the best time of year,” which is clearly true) but eventually settled on an unconventional-yet-simple dessert: a brûléed squash or sweet potato, riffing on the traditional Japanese winter snack.

The rest of the office was feeling a bit laconic, so I provided some additional incentive by telling them that if they didn’t give me a recommendation, I would have AI do it for them. That seemed to do the trick.

“This might make me sound like a narcissist but I randomly came across this book called Jerusalem the Golden by Margaret Drabble and immediately picked it up for obvious reasons,” said editor Jerusalem Demsas. “It’s a coming-of-age novel about a girl trying to break out of a provincial and constrained upbringing — but she finds out that no matter how far you run you can never escape your mother.”

“AI recommended that I recommend The Heart is a Lonely Hunter and I do, in fact, recommend it,” said senior editor John Thomason of Carson McCullers’s 1940 debut novel. “Alongside Ross McElwee’s 1986 film Sherman’s March, it’s probably the best piece of narrative art ever produced at least partially in (and, I would argue, at least partially by) Charlotte, North Carolina, a city with a well-known reputation for philistinism.”4

Video producer Justin Zuckerman also agreed with AI’s suggested recommendation: Ken Burns’ Baseball, which he’s about halfway through. “It’s around 18 hours of baseball history and lore, with folksy music and even folksier characters! It’s a great way to get excited about the postseason and also get your baseball fix during the winter months.”

Staff Writer Jeremiah Johnson said that he and his wife enjoyed watching “spoopy” — as in, “a mix of spooky and cute,” like The Nightmare Before Christmas — in the lead-up to Halloween.

“All horror media is implicitly fall-themed,” copy editor and fact checker Eli Richman noted, “and since he was robbed in The New York Times' top TV show list, I'll go ahead and recommend the works of Mike Flanagan. All of them…. The Haunting of Hill House gets all the love, and it's hard to argue it isn't deserved. But I'd reserve my biggest praise for Midnight Mass and Before I Wake.”

Sixty-three percent of 18-29 year-old Trump voters supported Congressional approval, though the sample size was too small to be considered good evidence.

In 2013, President Obama said he didn’t think he needed approval but he would seek approval for action in Syria and argued that the country would be “stronger if we take this course,” while this year, President Trump rejected the idea that Congress should even vote, complaining that it would threaten what he called, “My War Powers.”

item.title: The selfish war doctrine
item.content:encoded:
By Jeremiah Johnson

Welcome back to The Argument’s poll series, where we survey Americans on the issues everyone’s fighting about. Our full crosstabs are available behind the paywall at the end of this post. Our last surveys have asked about elite perception, AI, crime, gender issues, and much more.

You can see every single poll published by The Argument here.

Our full methodology can be read here.

—

Accepting his party’s nomination at the 2024 Republican National Convention, President Donald Trump promised that “the years of war, weakness, and chaos will be over” if he were elected.

He repeated some variation of this line dozens of times on the campaign trail. At a Bitcoin conference that same summer, he said, “I will end the endless wars. They never stop. Again, we had no wars. We had no new wars under your favorite president, President Trump. We had no new wars.”

Trump surrogates made the same argument frequently, as when former Democratic Rep. Tulsi Gabbard endorsed Trump, claiming that “[Trump] not only didn’t start any new wars, he took action to de-escalate and prevent wars” during his first term.

The standard story accepted by many pundits says that the GOP used to promote a more hawkish and pro-intervention foreign policy, but that Trump turned it into a more antiwar party — at least before he got bogged down in Iran (perhaps at the behest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu). The problem with this story is that it appears not to be true.

Trump has changed the right’s understanding of what American power is for. Bush-era Republicans paired their willingness to wage war with a belief that America should spread democracy, rebuild the countries it invaded, and sustain an international order. Trump rejected those obligations but retained the appetite for force — in his view, military action should deliver concrete gains for America, without saddling the nation with responsibilities to anyone else.

Subscribe now

In The Argument‘s new polling conducted Sept. 16-22, Republican voters share the president’s outlook: They remain enthusiastic about military action even as they distrust alliances and international institutions. That combination helps explain why a party that rejected Bush’s foreign policy still backs Trump’s war in Iran. The Republicans aren’t suddenly antiwar, they’re against liberal internationalism.

Though most Americans think the current war in Iran was a mistake, a strong majority of conservatives (61%) think it was right for the U.S. to start the war.

Whether you’re looking at 2024 Trump voters, self-identified conservatives, or Republicans, the story is roughly the same: Just over 60% support the current war in Iran. The narrative that Trump is betraying his base simply doesn’t match the polling data.

The right is also more likely than the left to approve of war in general and in a wide variety of scenarios. We asked poll respondents about past wars, and Republicans viewed America’s wars in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Vietnam far more favorably than Democrats did. Despite Trump’s criticism, a clear majority of Republicans still think it was correct to invade Iraq!

We also polled a number of hypothetical scenarios to decipher when voters think the U.S. is justified in taking military action. In every single scenario polled, a majority of Republicans said that military action was either always or usually justified — including a scenario where the action is just to promote America’s economic interests. And Republicans were more likely to approve of military action than Democrats in every scenario.

Trump has, of course, been more than happy to take military action in his second term. He sent special operations forces into Venezuela to kidnap the country’s dictator, Nicolas Maduro, and the administration has killed over 200 people in an ongoing series of military strikes, begun about a year ago, on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean. Last spring, he began an extensive bombing campaign of Houthi rebels in Yemen, striking the group more than 1,100 times and killing hundreds. All this was before he unilaterally launched a war on Iran in an attempt to overthrow the country’s government.

Now that the Iran war is dragging into its ninth month, many onetime Trump supporters have turned on him, seeing it as a betrayal. Joe Rogan lamented that “no one thought that we were gonna go into this prolonged war with Iran,” while Tucker Carlson radiated a sense of betrayal, calling the war “absolutely disgusting and evil.”

Trump, it turns out, hasn’t changed the Republican Party in the way many people assumed he had. So how did we get here?

The anti-war presidency that wasn’t

The easiest way to unpack this paradox is to realize that Trump did change Republican foreign policy — just not in the ways that people usually assume. I think it’s true that the political right in the Trump era is considerably more skeptical of military entanglements than the old neoconservative establishment was. But they’re not skeptical at all of using force.

Former President George W. Bush didn’t invade Iraq merely to stop a threat to the United States. His administration was committed to the project of nation-building and the idea of spreading democracy abroad, which is part of how U.S. forces ended up spending so many years in both Iraq and Afghanistan. However poorly those military adventures may have turned out, Bush-era Republican leaders took seriously the idea that American power came with great obligations. They believed in rebuilding countries America invaded, supporting the new governments, and constructing an international order that would promote liberal democracy.

Trump is allergic to the very idea of such obligations. He views international affairs as a zero-sum contest. In the 2015 speech announcing his candidacy, Trump said the U.S. had spent $2 trillion on Iraq, lost thousands of lives, and gotten “nothing,” while claiming he had warned: “Don’t hit Iraq,” because it would “totally destabilize the Middle East.” He would later repeatedly criticize the war, calling it a horrible decision and a “big, fat mistake.”1

Trump’s main criticism of the war in Iraq was that it cost the U.S. an enormous amount of money and lives and we didn’t get anything out of it, which is why he often advocated for seizing Iraq’s oil. “Take the oil” was a Trump obsession for decades before he entered public office — he advocated taking Iran’s oil by force all the way back in 1987. His fixation on using foreign policy to seize resources is also why he cut an oil deal with the new Venezuelan leadership after kidnapping Maduro.

In a major 2016 speech, Trump promised that America was getting out of the nation-building business. But in that same speech, he promised unquestioned American military dominance and said that the world is most peaceful “when America is strongest.”

The Republican base seems to agree with him. For decades, Republicans were more likely than Democrats to say that the U.S. should take an active role in world affairs. But that number has reversed in recent years, with the major flip happening in 2016 as Trump was running for president. In 2023, only 47% of Republicans agreed the U.S. should take an active role, compared with 70% of Democrats.

As we can see above, that decline isn’t driven by the Republican base suddenly becoming skeptical of war overall. Instead, it appears that conservatives are simply less likely to believe in the idea of international obligations. Republican support for the 2015 Paris Agreement on climate change declined after Trump’s first election, Republican support for defending South Korea has declined, and a growing share of Republicans also believe that America’s security alliances with European nations provide no benefits.

This skepticism is reflected in The Argument’s recent polling questions on attitudes toward NATO and the U.N., which finds that Republicans are far less favorably inclined towards international institutions than Democrats.

Trump doesn’t dislike military action. He just hates the idea that America might undertake such actions for any purpose higher than self-interest. If there’s a Trump doctrine, it’s a selfish war doctrine: Do what’s best for me. Show strength at all times. Don’t let allies, enemies, or anyone else take advantage of you. Don’t get bogged down by treaties or obligations, but make sure that other countries are terrified of what might happen if they cross you.

The median Republican seems to have absorbed this lesson. They’re still far more likely to favor military actions than Democrats — whether past, current, or hypothetical future actions. But they distrust our alliances, dislike international agreements, and don’t want to be burdened or constrained by formal commitments.

In the end, Trump didn’t dislodge the right’s hawkishness, but he did transform it. Republicans are now less interested in maintaining the world and more interested in dominating it, less willing to accept long-term obligations, but still eager to swing the biggest stick.

This leaves the Republican Party in a difficult position.The party’s base seems to fundamentally agree with the Trump doctrine of selfish war, but the Iran war is deeply unpopular with both liberals and moderates. And the war’s popularity continues to drop as it drags out longer and longer, leading to increases in fuel prices and the cost of living that the public directly blames on the war. Add those factors together, and it’s a major reason why the midterms are shaping up to be a disaster for the GOP.

item.title: What if dictators never died?
item.description: I don't want to live forever but I'll take 150 years
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

This week on The Argument podcast, Matt Yglesias and I are joined by ChinaTalk’s Jordan Schneider to discuss all things China and AI. Paid subscribers can watch or listen to the episode ad free here and read the transcript at the end of this post. Free subscribers can watch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Can we cure human frailty?

As we discover treatments for various diseases that used to reliably cut us down, humans are living longer than ever. The real question is whether curing all diseases would mean we get to live forever.

Before doing research for this essay, I believed that sometimes people just died of old age — that is, the human body is frail and just sort of stops working. That could mean cells stop replicating or become less functional, tissue loses its ability to repair everyday damage, or some other breakdown.

However, I was surprised to learn that there’s a lot of controversy over this common intuition.

Share

“Do centenarians die healthy?” is a study of 40 very old people. Researchers conducted autopsies to determine if there was some hidden cause of death, even if the deceased was described as healthy beforehand. In every single case, the doctors were able to attribute death to disease — usually cardiovascular or respiratory conditions. It’s not certain that those diseases were the cause of death, but it does cast doubt on the accepted folk wisdom about death from old age. Several independent autopsy studies found a similar pattern.

It seems at least theoretically possible to achieve immortality by preventing all diseases and replacing organs as they fail — though that proposition will get increasingly difficult as transplants extend to brains.

Actual immortality may be unlikely, but could humans eventually figure out how to keep our bodies going for a couple hundred years? That seems entirely plausible — but a world in which people can live for centuries is also one in which dictators can rule for centuries.

The undead dictator

Immortality may be the last thing you want to hear a dictator contemplate, but last year, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were overheard on a hot mic discussing just that.

“Before it’s said to be very rare to live up to 70, and now it’s said that you are still a child at 70,” said Xi (through an interpreter).

“In a few decades, as biotechnology continues to develop, human organs will continue to be transplanted and people will become younger and perhaps even achieve immortality,” noted Putin, also through an interpreter.

Xi later mused on predictions that humans “may be able to live up to 150 years old.”

World leaders are getting older. This is in part a function of aging electorates, but one report by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development showed that in autocracies, leaders were 26 years older than the median adult in 2023, compared to just 19 years in 1960. (Democracies saw no meaningful change.)

The explanation centers on turnover: The average tenure for an autocrat rose from roughly four years to over 10 over the last century, whereas for democratic leaders, tenure has fallen.

Recently, Xi came to Washington to meet with President Donald Trump. While little of substance seems to have emerged, ChinaTalk’s Jordan Schneider joined the latest episode of The Argument podcast to discuss the visit and its implications.

One takeaway was the visual evidence of human frailty on display between the two leaders: “Two most powerful countries in the world are ruled by one guy who’s 73 and one guy who’s 80. And they kind of don’t walk great anymore and need naps,” said Schneider.

When the end of one life feels like the end of history

There are many reasons the West rejected authoritarian governing models, but one core reason is that even if you get a very good king, there’s always the problem of succession.1

Aristotle questioned, “even if one held that royal government is best for states, what is to be the position as regards the king’s children?” After praising Rome’s comparatively good emperors, Edward Gibbon, in his canonical work The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, observed: “They must often have recollected the instability of a happiness which depended on the character of a single man.”

Natural death is a stabilizing force. For hungry would-be leaders waiting in the wings, the inevitable death of the leader reduces the incentive for assassination.

Subscribe now

We see a version of this dynamic mirrored in democracies as well — particularly in the “gerontocracy” discourse. As the average age of tenured faculty and politicians in key leadership roles has gone up, those waiting in the wings have grown increasingly restless. American universities removed mandatory retirement policies for tenured faculty in 1994, which sharply reduced retirement rates. As Yale Law professor Samuel Moyn characterized the situation, “younger academics today regard those elders much as serfs on the brink of the French Revolution saw the noble lords.” (A bit hyperbolic, but I take his core point.)

In 2018, a rebellion of young House Democrats led by Reps. Seth Moulton and Tim Ryan was trying to prevent then-78-year-old Nancy Pelosi’s return as speaker. In order to gain support, Pelosi acquiesced to term limits and described herself as the “bridge to the next generation of leaders.”

Natural death is also a solution for the subjects of tyrants. Revolt and exit are costly and sometimes ineffective — but if your autocrat is old enough, maybe you can just wait him out. Two of the worst dictators of the 20th century, Mao Zedong and Joseph Stalin, died to their nations’ great relief.

Ismikhan Rahimov, an Azerbaijani teacher sentenced to 25 years in the Gulag, later told his story in a magazine, writing that he held onto the expectation of Stalin’s death:

“I was convinced that as soon as Stalin died, a new policy would take effect in Russia. That’s the way it had always been throughout Russia’s entire history. When the Czar was overthrown, a new policy was established. Besides, Stalin was already 70 years old at the time I was arrested. I knew his end was coming. So I knew that we would come back. Little did I know, however, how long it would take, and what difficult circumstances I would have to live through, until that day.”

One month after Mao’s death in 1976, his successors arrested Mao’s proteges — the Gang of Four — marking the end of the Cultural Revolution. They were charged with many crimes that Mao himself was also responsible for, including “keeping a nation of 800 million living in constant fear” and “ruining the education system” and “preventing a single poem or play from being printed much less published without their approval.”

In many ways, they were forced to pay for their own crimes as well as Mao’s.

The Chinese Communist Party’s 1981 historical resolution acknowledged Mao’s ultimate responsibility, but immediately after doing so, it argued that Mao’s dark age was “the error of a great proletarian revolutionary.” While the chairman “paid constant attention to overcoming shortcomings in the life of the Party and state,” late in life he “confused right and wrong and the people with the enemy.”

Meanwhile, the Gang of Four were accused of “taking advantage of Comrade Mao Zedong’s errors [and] committ[ing] many crimes behind his back, bringing disaster to the country and the people.” Mao’s death gave his successors room to abandon some of his most disastrous policies while continuing to celebrate him as a great revolutionary.

While Mao’s death famously did not pave the road to democracy in China, there are more hopeful examples. According to one historian, opposition to Francisco Franco’s dictatorial regime in Spain was willing to wait for Franco’s death, much to the chagrin of young Basque activists. Franco’s opponents could hope to outlast him even if they could not overthrow him. That calculation looks very different if a dictator can expect another century in power.

Of course, death is not a panacea.

Many dictators die, and their countries fall into chaos and civil war or peacefully transition to another dictator. But a dictator’s death does create an opening to escape that particular ruler’s regime.

Share

Some autocrats are in fact better than others. China is not some paragon of liberalism and democracy, but life for everyday people became substantially better after Mao’s death — political persecution declined significantly and Deng Xiaoping’s eventual ascendancy ushered in an era of economic growth that raised living standards more than any other event in human history.

Do you want to live forever?

Dictators are a highly selected bunch and probably score higher in areas like megalomania than the rest of us — but nevertheless, I am curious how readers of The Argument score on whether or not they want to live forever!

In a 2015 YouGov poll of British adults, just 28% of people said they would like to live forever if they could. In a 2025 Pew poll, Americans were asked how long they would live if they could choose, and the average age was 91; just 7% said they would like to live to 120 or beyond. (Forever was not offered as an option.)

Part of what’s going on here is that some people don’t want to live a long time if they’re living diminished lives in poor health. Another is that one’s friends and family don’t always get to come along. Other survey evidence indicates that if one or both of those matters were squared away, higher numbers of people would take the longevity pill.

An extra century with the people you love seems great — as long as it’s not another century under autocratic rule.

Today’s podcast with Schneider and my co-host Matt Yglesias ranges far afield from longevity. We get into how Chinese and American political leaders are using AI and how the technology is shaping geopolitical crises. It’s a really fun episode, and it’s great to have a bona fide expert on to gab with us about geopolitics.

Download wherever you get your podcasts!

The Argument. Libbing out.

Paying subscribers can find the transcript for this post beneath the paywall.

New episodes post every Thursday.

For an ad-free version and full transcript, subscribe at TheArgumentMag.com.

  • Around 26:15, Jordan says China was growing at a rate of 8% to 9% in the 2000s, 5% to 6% in the 2010s, and between 0.5% and 1.5% for the past six years. According to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, the country grew at a rate of 8.3% to 14.2% in the 2000s, 6.1% to 10.6% in the 2010s, and 2.3% to 8.6% in the 2020s.

  • Around 27:50, Jordan says the U.S. has an unemployment rate of 3%. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ latest report, the unemployment rate reached 4.2% in September.

The Argument has not polled this question specifically, but in Sept. 2025, 43% of voters said AI has had a positive impact on their own life and 32% said it has a positive impact on society. In July 2026, 55% said they at least somewhat enjoyed using AI.

item.title: The MAGA realignment realigns
item.description: The numbers behind the Trump coalition’s crackup
item.content:encoded:
By Lakshya Jain

To virtually anyone watching the 2024 election, one of the biggest shocks of the cycle was the way young and Hispanic voters zoomed toward Donald Trump.

Two years later, it’s difficult to find signs of the president retaining any of that once-mythical strength.

Share

Through aggregating and analyzing the surveys we’ve done at The Argument, we have been able to reconstruct a spectacularly detailed picture of both the American electorate at large and the likely electorate of 2026. This trove of data allows us to see Trump’s approval and voting intent for each subgroup. And it tells us that Democrats are making titanic gains among the groups they initially lost ground with in 2024, as young and Hispanic voters abandon Trump at dizzying speeds.

Whether because of disillusionment over his foreign policy, anger over his immigration agenda, or disappointment over the way he has handled the cost-of-living crisis, Trump’s approval has cratered spectacularly. His net approval with Hispanic voters sits at -37 with registered voters, and at -39 with likely voters. Meanwhile, the picture is even uglier with young voters, as his approval sits at a shocking -45 with registered voters and -50 with likely ones.

Two things are happening as a result. First, a lot of voters are simply switching sides. Among all registered voters between 2024 and 2026, Democrats have gained over 11 percentage points of margin with Hispanics and young voters alike, which exceeds the leftward national swing by a few points.

But our polling also found something else: a lot of the conservative voters who remain unwilling to vote for Democrats are also so angry at Trump that they have no intention of showing up in 2026. We see this in the delta between the likely voter electorate and the registered-voter electorate. Even though registered voters are a less Democratic sample, Trump’s approval is the same in both groups. That means the registered voters who are unlikely to vote are disproportionately Republican-leaning voters who disapprove of Trump.1 This takes the swings projected for the midterm from notable to colossal.

When we compared the margins of the 2024 election to those of the likely 2026 electorate, Democrats picked up 17 percentage points in net margin with Hispanics, as well as 23 points with voters under the age of 30.

In the case of Hispanics, these projected 2026 margins are on par with Joe Biden’s 2020 numbers.2 Meanwhile, with young voters, you’d have to go back to either the 2018 blue wave or Barack Obama’s 2008 landslide for the last time Democrats saw numbers this high.

Subscribe now

It would be a mistake to look at this and think that the Democratic problems of 2024 are all solved. Voters who sit out the 2026 midterms may return for the 2028 presidential election. And among all registered voters — not just the ones likely to vote this November — the shift toward Democrats is considerably smaller, even though Trump is similarly unpopular in both groups. That suggests a substantial and disproportionate chunk of the voters who have abandoned the president remain unwilling to vote for Democrats.

In particular, when it comes to the full electorate of registered voters, the margin by which people disapprove of Trump is much larger than Democrats’ lead over Republicans. That gap is especially large with many subgroups, including young and white noncollege voters, suggesting again that dissatisfaction with Trump doesn’t necessarily translate into votes for Democrats.

That’s the sort of thing that calls into question just how durable either side’s electoral position really is. It means that these voters remain up for grabs in the next election despite how intensely they’ve soured on the president, giving both sides glimmers of hope in 2028. After all, while it’s clear that most voters now dislike Trump, it’s not yet so clear that they would vote for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, or Kamala Harris over Secretary of State Marco Rubio or Vice President JD Vance in 2028.

When I see the chart we’ve assembled above, I see a myriad of potential outcomes.

In one, Democrats could sweep 2028 in the same way that they dominated 2008. Disillusioned white working-class voters, Hispanics, and young voters could rocket to the left over disappointment with the outgoing Republican president’s handling of foreign wars, cost of living, and healthcare.

In another, a tight election could result in a narrow Republican win, with just enough voters holding their nose for a different kind of Republican candidate against an unappealing Democrat.

Those are two wildly different outcomes, but in many ways, the uncertainty is the point. Though the story of 2026 may be largely written by now, the story of 2028 certainly isn’t.

But this is still a very different type of discussion than the one we were having in 2024. Axios‘ youth-vote analysis declared, “A big chunk of the future electorate is MAGA red” and claimed “lasting power” for MAGA. Data scientist David Shor, speaking on The Ezra Klein Show, described young people as “potentially the most conservative generation that we’ve experienced maybe in 50 to 60 years.” Few predicted that the right-wing youth revolution of 2024 was potentially just a blip on the radar.

Meanwhile, endless pages of ink were spilled on the loss of Democratic standing with Hispanics. Discussing Republican gains in heavily Hispanic communities, pollster Patrick Ruffini argued that “the FDR coalition is being dismantled piece by piece and being reassembled in Donald Trump’s GOP.”

The change we’re seeing doesn’t make those autopsies any less correct or valuable, but it does remind us that the certainty can sometimes just be an artifact of a lack of data. With two years between elections, each race is analyzed and scrutinized endlessly with a fine-toothed comb in the hopes of avoiding or predicting the next surprise.

But at the end of the day, the choices that parties make really do matter. And had Trump made some different ones, we probably wouldn’t be having this conversation today.

Subscribe now

METHODOLOGY

To assemble these estimates, we combined data from all of the surveys performed by The Argument over the course of 2026. First, a likely voter screen was created for each survey. The likely voter screen takes every respondent’s demographic and voting history and calculates a probability that they will vote in 2026. It then aligns this with probabilistic turnout scores from self-expressed vote likelihood and rakes this to the likely 2026 electorate, calculated via historical demographic turnout data from a Catalist voter file sample, in order to estimate respondents’ likelihood of voting.

Then, the pooled survey file is fitted among 2024 voters to have demographic shares and Verasight panel-profiled votes match the margins in Catalist’s 2024 What Happened report on the following factors: race by age, race by education, and race by gender (for white, Black, and Hispanic voters). It is also weighted to match the report’s margins for age and to match the actual, certified election results by region. This allows us to anchor our own 2026 estimates by ensuring that the 2024 vote margins of our demographics align with actual, validated external measures. Every registered voter is also weighted to the Catalist voter file sample’s benchmarks on white/nonwhite by modeled party.

Respondent likely voter weights are then rescaled by the amount they shifted by during the recalled margin rake, and the likely electorate is then restratified across demographics to align with the initial likely electorate screen.

1

It’s especially notable that Trump’s approval is better among the likely electorate than the full electorate of registered voters for noncollege whites.

2

It should be noted, though, that these are still well short of the margins that Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton put up.

item.title: Marco Rubio flunks Western Civ
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Jerusalem Demsas

Earlier this week, in front of the ruins of the Acropolis, a son of Cuban immigrants claimed the mantle of Western civilization.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood on the hill where, once a year, the Athenian assembly voted on whether to banish any citizen who had grown too powerful. There he gave a speech in praise of “the great man: the exceptional individual who obtains immortality through his own deeds.” Rubio argued that the ancient Greeks idealized this type and organized all of civic life around “contest, ambition, competition.” Their thumos, “the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride,” was “the heart of great civilization.”

In Rubio’s telling, the fire is inherited. The greatest Americans, he says, “carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers — born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom.” Rubio casts this inheritance in the language of bloodlines, making a civilization of ideas sound like a family pedigree. Yet, for something supposedly in his blood, “Christendom” trips awkwardly off his tongue; twice he pronounces it like a child encountering the word on the page for the first time. (“Chris, ten, dom.”)

Rubio argues that the modern West has lost touch with the spirit that animated the Greeks: “Over time, we in the West came to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional. We felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world. Our prosperity somehow became a source of guilt.”

I am a big fan of Western civilization. That’s why I refuse to let the Rubios of the world mangle its history and values. He has the Greeks backward on two counts.

Let’s start with thumos. The philosophers Rubio cites did prize spiritedness, but Plato thought those impulses needed to be governed by reason. In The Republic, thumos is reason’s “ally”: It should help us act on our judgement, rather than overpower it. Plato argued that when thumos, or the pursuit of honor, becomes a society’s highest goal, as it was in Sparta, that was the first stop on the road to tyranny.

In the Laws, Plato’s last word on politics, the highest good is “peace one with another and friendly feeling,” and courage ranks “no higher than fourth” among the virtues. When Plato sorted the world’s peoples by their dominant trait, he gave spiritedness to those the Greeks saw as barbarians (Thracians and Scythians) and love of learning to the Greeks. The very trait that Rubio venerates was, in Plato’s account, more characteristic of the people Greeks considered barbarians.

Athens built that lesson into its institutions. The Athenians were terrified by excessive ambition, which is why they created restraints. They were so worried about the destructiveness of unchecked great men that they reserved the right to banish them from Athens.

Rubio also provides a confused recounting of Greek “nationalism.” Modern western nations have treated nationalism like a “dirty word,” but the Greeks can apparently teach us better; they “knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation.”

But the Greeks famously had no nations to be loyal to. They had cities that fought against one another for most of the classical age. James Madison laments that disunity in Federalist 18, and in Federalist 9, Alexander Hamilton writes that it’s “impossible to read the history of the petty republics of Greece” without “horror and disgust.” The solution? A “firm Union.”

When Athens did pursue “national power” without apology, historians chronicled the devastating results: Athens massacred the islanders of Melos for refusing to submit, lost its army and fleet invading Sicily, and eventually surrendered. The Greek lesson about nationalism is a warning for the future, not a playbook handed down through the centuries.

In The End of History and the Last Man, Francis Fukuyama invoked thumos because he worried that the very spiritedness Rubio celebrates could turn against liberal democracy. Citizens dissatisfied with modernity’s comforts might “struggle for the sake of struggle” — against peace, prosperity, and democracy itself. Perhaps Rubio is auditioning for the role of Last Man in search of a struggle.

Rubio’s second major error is his account of the role of kinship, and here Rubio’s speech refutes itself in a single aside. “The city where our Constitution was born — Philadelphia — is itself a Greek name,” Rubio notes, in order to firm up his connection between America and ancient Greece. For Plutarch, whom Rubio calls the Federalist Papers’ most-cited author1, philadelphia meant the love between actual siblings.2

American history tells a different story. When the Quaker William Penn gave the name to Pennsylvania’s capital, he was calling on the early Christian idea of brotherly love, which extended to strangers: “Be devoted to one another in brotherly love,” the apostle Paul wrote to a church of Jews and gentiles.

Penn was founding a refuge for Quakers, Huguenots, Mennonites, Lutherans, and Catholics whose only common ancestry was religious persecution. It’s ludicrous to cite the name he chose to claim that Americans are united only by blood. Philadelphia is a Greek word for a Christian idea, chosen by an Englishman for a city built on the premise that strangers could be brothers.

This is the West that Rubio belongs to.

In 2019, Rubio went on the PBS genealogy show Finding Your Roots and discovered that he wasn’t the first in his family to graduate law school. That honor likely belonged to his great-great-great grandfather who graduated from the University of Granada with a law degree in 1786. On his mother’s side, Rubio has a great-great-great-grandmother who was Native American.

Rubio’s claim to Western civilization does not run through a prosecutor in 18th-century Seville. It runs through the ideas that shaped his life and the institutions of the country his parents chose when they immigrated from Cuba. Abraham Lincoln said as much in 1858, defending immigrants with no ancestral tie to the founders; they have a right to claim the Declaration “as though they were blood of the blood, and flesh of the flesh of the men who wrote that Declaration, and so they are.”

Holding these views does not make one any less of a patriot. Lincoln was a nationalist, and so were the men who wrote NATO’s charter, which pledges to defend “the freedom, common heritage and civilisation of their peoples, founded on the principles of democracy, individual liberty and the rule of law.” The argument isn’t about whether you should love America (you should) but what makes you an American to begin with.

The explicit purpose of Rubio’s visit — the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue — flew in the face of the ideas he delivered in his speech. The agenda covered F-35s and F-16 upgrades, routing American natural gas into Europe through Greece, and a new counterterrorism information-sharing agreement. Every agenda item was a product of the liberal international order: open trade between nations, collective defense among allies, and law-enforcement cooperation built on the shared assumption that two democracies can trust each other’s courts and police.

Rubio is hardly the first member of the Trump administration to begin flirting with blood-and-soil nationalism. Vice president JD Vance has argued that America is not a set of principles but a homeland measured by the generations buried in its earth.

Some hoped Rubio could chart a different course for the Republican Party once President Trump is off the scene. But this speech confirms that the leading lights of the right are increasingly in thrall to a version of Vance’s post-liberalism, an anti-American ideology that mangles our histories, customs, and values in service of a pedigree so narrow that its own champion had to leave out his parents’ birthplace to claim it.

Subscribe now

Midterm update

Lakshya Jain, our director of political data, uses data from The Argument’s polling operation to inform the Split Ticket 2026 House and Senate models. Here’s his update on the state of play this week:

The picture in the House is stable, as Democrats remain heavy favorites to win back the chamber with a win probability of 89%. That’s an even better situation than they faced in 2018. In the Senate, Democrats have a slight but growing edge, with a 65% chance of winning the chamber — that’s an all-time high for this cycle. The picture suddenly looks so good for them that even Kansas is barely in the Republican column at the moment. We’ve been here before, and the model has a lot of uncertainty baked in because of the potential for a systematic polling miss. But even with that, you’d rather be the Democrats.

These models update every day; bookmark this page to see the odds of each party taking the House and the Senate.

Top stories this week, by Maibritt Henkel

Accelerating the federal permitting process is great news for clean energy and grid expansion, but not all climate groups are happy about the Senate bill introduced last week. The Center for Biological Diversity (CBD) has strongly opposed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act on the grounds that it rolls back environmental protections and allows for fossil fuel expansion. Jerusalem Demsas saw this coming. She argues that the CBD has a long and well-documented history of shutting down infrastructure projects, even ones that would significantly reduce carbon emissions, in the name of protecting endangered species. But does the organization really want more amphipods in Rock Creek Park? Or does it just want fewer humans?

Technology is not in itself progress. Derek Thompson reminded us of this fact in his guest essay this week. The printing press, the power loom, the radio — all of these technologies would go on to change society in positive ways, but only because government and civil society channeled them toward human well-being through regulation and adaptation. Before British cities developed the infrastructure to handle the sudden influx of rural workers, the Industrial Revolution was a complete and utter nightmare. First there were piles of human waste rotting in every basement; then there were sewage systems and paved streets. The AI era now needs an institutional and regulatory response that turns disaster into progress.

While the story of the 2026 midterms seems more or less written by now, the story of 2028 certainly isn’t. In his column this week, Lakshya Jain laid out what we know so far about the electorate that will determine the next president in two years. The numbers currently bode well for Democrats. The voters who secured Trump’s victory last time around are now turning on him in droves: net approval with registered Hispanic voters sits at -37. With young voters, that number is a startling -45. Time will tell whether Democrats manage to convert this disapproval into votes for their own side.

🌟Abundance Wins of the Week🌟

  • There is a new kind of solar panel gaining ground in the U.S., driven by a push to beat China in clean-energy manufacturing. These so-called tandem panels combine a mineral perovskite top layer with a silicon bottom layer and can generate up to 25% more energy than standard panels. This technology would allow energy companies to produce more electricity using the same number of resources.

  • The 2026 Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel earlier this week for optogenetics, a technique that Reuters described as using “light to control individual nerve cells in the brain.” The technology is already in early clinical trials for blindness.
